title: Optimal summary statistics to constrain w0waCDM with the DESI BGS
comment: This document is part of the Proceedings of the 60th Rencontres de Moriond, Cosmology
summary: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is the first stage-4 spectroscopic instrument installed on the 4-m Mayall Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. It contains 5000 robotically positioned fibers, allowing the measurement of as many galaxy spectra in one observation (~20 minutes). The data acquisition (2021--2028) aims at constraining the cosmological parameters, and especially the parameters describing the evolution of the dark energy with time. However, standard clustering analysis based on 2-point statistics only capture the Gaussian information of the matter density field, while the analytical models used to match these statistical probe are limited to quasi-linear scales, as they are based on perturbation theory. Therefore, the non-Gaussian and non-linear information of the density field is not exploited. To go beyond these limitations, several alternative clustering methods have been developed that rely on a simulation-based pipeline. In this presentation, we focus on the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey, a magnitude-limited sample of bright galaxies in the redshift range of 0.1 < z < 0.4. We present how accessing the non-linear and non-Gaussian information of the density field allows around 40% improvement on the constraints of some $Λ$CDM parameters. We are also extending the method to constrain w0waCDM in order to improve DESI's sensibility at low redshift where the Universe is dominated by dark energy.

title: Gravitational Production of Non-minimally Coupled Vector Dark Matter in Warm Inflation
summary: We study the purely gravitational production of a massive vector dark matter with a non-minimal coupling to the Einstein tensor, $ξG_{μν}X^μX^ν$, in warm inflation. The background, $V=λφ^4$ with a dissipation coefficient linear in temperature, is constrained by CMB observations and parametrized by the dissipation ratio $10^{-4}\le Q_0\le1$. We consider both unavoidable production channels: freeze-in from the Standard Model bath through graviton exchange, and cosmological gravitational particle production (CGPP). For freeze-in, we compute the scattering amplitudes including the contact interaction induced by $ξ$, which enhances the production of light dark matter through the longitudinal mode and suppresses that of heavy dark matter through destructive interference. For CGPP, the slow-roll parameter is not small during warm inflation, which enhances the production of light dark matter by up to three orders of magnitude relative to cold inflation. Combining both channels, CGPP excludes most of the light freeze-in branch, leaving $m_X\lesssim2.4\times10^{-5}$ GeV, a narrow window around $10^{10}$ GeV for strong dissipation, and $m_X\gtrsim10^{14}$--$10^{15}$ GeV. Only the heavy branch remains viable for all $|ξ|\lesssim1$.

title: FAIR Universe Weak Lensing ML Uncertainty Challenge: Dataset and Cosmological Inference Competition
comment: 10+7 pages, 2+4 figures, 2+1 tables. Key results of the NeurIPS 2025 FAIR Universe Weak Lensing ML Challenge Phase 1. The challenge dataset is publicly available at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/20056065. Challenge GitHub repository: https://github.com/FAIR-Universe/Cosmology_Challenge
summary: Weak gravitational lensing is a powerful cosmological probe that enables direct mapping of the matter distribution and precise constraints on the fundamental parameters governing structure formation in the universe. In recent years, machine learning has shown strong potential for extracting cosmological information from weak-lensing data beyond traditional summary statistics. However, progress has been limited by the lack of standardized benchmarks that capture the complexity of the dataset, simulator imperfections, and various systematic biases encountered in realistic analyses. To address this gap, we present the FAIR Universe Weak Lensing Machine Learning Uncertainty Challenge, one of the NeurIPS 2025 competitions, as a benchmark dataset and evaluation study. Our dataset reflects realistic weak-lensing observations, incorporating multiple systematic biases, and thereby providing a controlled testbed for robust cosmological inference under uncertainties. We summarize the main methodological advances developed by the winners of our challenge, including data augmentation with conditional optimal transport, an AI-agent-driven approach for parameter inference, ensemble learning, Vision Transformer-based architectures, and physics-informed feature integration. By unifying the benchmark dataset and the winning solutions, this work provides a community resource for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for weak lensing cosmology and, more broadly, for scientific inference under systematic uncertainties.

title: Constraining Cosmic Deceleration using the Solar System
comment: 21 pages with 2 figures, comments very welcome
summary: We investigate whether Solar System dynamics can provide independent constraints on the present day cosmological deceleration parameter $q_0$, offering a complementary approach to conventional cosmological probes. By relating cosmic acceleration to a weak Hooke type radial perturbation, we derive bounds using planetary perihelion precession, trans-Neptunian objects, and Oort cloud dynamics. We obtain relatively robust planetary bounds of $|q_0|\lesssim 10^9$, while the outer Solar System yields potentially stronger, albeit more model dependent, constraints approaching $10^5$. Through Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation and sensitivity analyses, we explore the statistical robustness of these estimates and their dependence on orbital measurements. Finally, we demonstrate how future precision astrometry and outer planet missions could improve these limits by several orders of magnitude, establishing Solar System dynamics as a complementary laboratory for probing cosmological acceleration.

title: Probing circumstellar interaction with spectroscopy of ZTF hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae
summary: Hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae (H-rich SLSNe) are rare, exceptionally luminous transients. Most exhibit narrow Balmer emission and can be further classified as SLSNe-IIn, indicating interaction with dense circumstellar material (CSM). We present and analyse 304 optical spectra of 106 H-rich SLSNe observed by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). We examine their spectral evolution and Balmer-line properties, and model the H$α$ profiles using Monte Carlo electron-scattering calculations. Of the 106 objects, 105 exhibit narrow Balmer emission consistent with SLSN-IIn classifications, including six with additional Ia-CSM-like characteristics and three with possible flash-ionisation features; the remaining one object exhibits only broad Balmer emission and is classified as a SLSN-II. Post-peak Balmer profiles range from approximately symmetric, exponential profiles to asymmetric profiles with prominent blue excesses or shoulders. Objects with Balmer line blue excess favour higher fitted photon-emitting shell velocities and tend to be fainter than those with persistently symmetric profiles. The H$α$ pseudo-equivalent width (pEW) and FWHM of SLSNe-IIn overlap with those of lower-luminosity SNe IIn, while the pEW evolution is more diverse than in the broad-lined SLSN-II comparison sample. Our SLSNe-IIn sample's median Balmer decrement increases from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterwards, remaining consistently below that of the comparison Ia-CSM sample. We identify no Balmer-line morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn in the available comparison with lower-luminosity SNe IIn, although some SLSNe-IIn exhibit prolonged high-ionisation emission. Our results also support interaction with dense CSM formed through enhanced pre-explosion mass loss. We also highlight a possible hidden Ia-CSM population among luminous H-rich interacting SNe.

title: Is Dark Energy Inhomogeneous?
comment: 25 pages with 1 figure, comments very welcome
summary: The discovery of dark matter deficient galaxies motivates a fundamental question: Could sufficiently large regions of the Universe be deficient in dark energy as well? We investigate this possibility by developing a phenomenological framework that distinguishes genuine dark energy deficiencies from ordinary matter voids through nonlinear expansion, coherent peculiar velocities and density-momentum correlations. We show that a $10\%$ dark energy deficiency can suppress the expansion of a representative nonlinear void by approximately $2.7\%$, generating peculiar velocity residuals of order $60$-$100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ across scales of $30$-$50\, Mpc$. Intriguingly, we find that deficiencies of order $20\%$ extending over several hundred megaparsecs could also influence the locally inferred Hubble constant, potentially contributing to the $H_0$ tension, subject to stringent isotropy and dynamical consistency constraints. We identify observational strategies involving DESI, Rubin, peculiar velocity surveys, and cosmic void catalogues, opening a new avenue for testing whether the dark energy driving cosmic acceleration is truly homogeneous.

title: Current Closure and Gamma-Ray Signatures of Spark-Gap and Current-Sheet Activities in Radiative Black Hole Magnetospheres
summary: We investigate the evolution of an axisymmetric black hole magnetosphere using general relativistic particle-in-cell simulations, focusing on its global current structure, variability, and radiative effects. We include inverse-Compton (IC) scattering of ambient photons and subsequent two-photon pair production, and compare simulations with and without synchrotron-curvature (SC) radiation reaction. Starting from an axisymmetric vertical magnetic field, the system develops a polar spark gap and a variable equatorial current sheet that together sustain the global poloidal current. For the parameters explored in this study, we observe that the spark gap oscillates upon the onset of SC cooling, whereas the current sheet is less sensitive to radiative cooling. Time-dependent electric fields in the return-current layer trigger magnetic-field rearrangement followed by magnetic reconnection. Cross-correlation analysis finds no significant correlation between the two regions' variability, suggesting dynamical independence. We further perform post-processing ray-tracing calculations to evaluate the radiative efficiencies of the IC and SC processes. High-energy particles dominate the bolometric luminosity, which reaches up to 1 percent of the Blandford-Znajek luminosity for SC emission and 0.1 percent for IC emission. The relative IC luminosity to SC is higher at lower viewing angles because particle momenta are more anisotropic near the pole than near the equator, due to efficient acceleration along the local magnetic field lines. Together with energetic estimates, these results suggest that both regions can contribute to high-energy emission in active galactic nuclei, with spark-gap photons reaching the sub-TeV regime.

title: Detecting Baryon Acoustic Oscillations from Galaxy Clusters: Distance Constraints
summary: We present a measurement of the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) feature using the largest galaxy cluster sample with spectroscopic redshift information to date, comprising 169,679 clusters selected from the WH24 catalogue based on the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. We measure the two-point correlation function in two redshift bins, $0.17\leq z<0.35$ and $0.35\leq z<0.5$, corresponding to effective redshifts of $z_{\rm eff}=0.25$ and $0.43$, with the BAO feature detected at approximately the $4σ$ level or above in both bins. By fitting the measured correlation functions, we obtain dilation parameters of $α=0.97\pm0.07$ and $α=1.01\pm0.04$, corresponding to volume-averaged distance measurements of $D_V/r_d=6.70\pm0.48$ and $D_V/r_d=11.25\pm0.47$, respectively. Using the Planck 2018 sound horizon calibration, we obtain $H_0=66.6 \pm 4.9 \,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ within the flat $Λ$CDM framework. We further combine our cluster BAO measurements with cosmic microwave background and Pantheon+ Type Ia supernova observations to constrain dynamical dark energy within the Chevallier--Polarski--Linder parametrization. The resulting constraints are consistent with $Λ$CDM, which lies within the $68\%$ joint credible region in the $w_0$--$w_a$ plane. Our results demonstrate the potential of galaxy clusters as complementary tracers for BAO measurements and cosmological constraints.

title: Faint Thermonuclear Transients from the Double Detonations of Common White Dwarfs
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 1 table; submitted to ApJ
summary: The double detonation model is a viable channel to explain many observed Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), with thin helium shelled white dwarf (WD) progenitors of 0.9--1.1 M$_\odot$ reproducing normal SNe Ia observables. Recent work has also shown that all C/O WDs $\leq$ 1.0 M$_\odot$ can sustain a helium shell detonation that triggers a detonation of the underlying core. As WDs of lower masses (0.5--0.7 M$_\odot$) far outnumber those at higher mass, it is important to explore their double detonation outcomes. To that end, we conducted multidimensional double detonation simulations of low mass C/O cores with very thin helium shells, finding explosion outcomes that differ non-trivially from those at higher masses. Not surprisingly, their cores are incompletely burned with low yields of radioactive elements. Though still formally unbound in isolation, some of the ejecta could remain bound to a nearby companion. In addition, the offset initiation of the core detonation wave and its failure to burn through the entire core lead to a very asymmetric distribution of $^{56}$Ni that creates dramatically viewing angle-dependent light curves and spectra. We find that the peak bolometric luminosities for the same explosion vary up to nearly 2 magnitudes over the sky, and that the spectra and light curves from these models are within the range of faint SNe Iax. In particular, our 0.50 M$_\odot$ models agree well with the photometry of SNe Iax 2008ha and 2024vjm.

title: Vacuum energy interacting with dark matter and dark radiation: alleviating the $H_0$-$S_8$ seesaw
summary: Extensions of $Λ$CDM that raise $H_0$ with additional energy before recombination, such as dark radiation and early dark energy (EDE), also raise $S_8$. We study whether a late-time energy exchange between the vacuum and the dark sector can offset this increase. The coupling rate scales as $\bar m H^α$ and is negligible before recombination for $α\le -2$; the energy is transferred along the four-velocity of geodesic cold dark matter, so the dark matter produced by the vacuum carries no density perturbation and slows the growth of structure. We add the exchange to dark radiation ($\bar m\tildeΛ$CDM) and to a one-parameter EDE model ($\bar m$EDE), and constrain the models with Planck 2018, DESI DR2 BAO and Pantheon+ data (CBS), and with the SH0ES calibration added (CBSH) to test the exchange when $H_0$ is held at a high value. For CBS the posteriors favour an energy flow from the vacuum into dark matter at 1.8-2.7$σ$, and the exchange lowers $S_8$ by 0.02-0.08 but does not raise $H_0$: $\bar m\tildeΛ$CDM gives $H_0 = 68.83 \pm 0.91$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, 3.1$σ$ below SH0ES. For CBSH the exchange removes the increase of $S_8$ caused by dark radiation, giving $S_8 = 0.800 \pm 0.016$ at $H_0 = 71.34 \pm 0.70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, and about a third of that caused by EDE for $α= -2$, with the coupling at 1.1-2.0$σ$. The reduction of $S_8$ is concentrated at $z \lesssim 0.3$: at the redshifts probed by KiDS-Legacy the lensing amplitude decreases by only 1-2%, the shear $χ^2$ of the dark-radiation models changes by less than 3, and the exchange reduces but does not remove the excess shear $χ^2$ of EDE. A late-time exchange can therefore offset part of the $S_8$ increase of early-time solutions, but it does not ease the Hubble tension, and current data do not require it.

title: Polarization Signatures of Magnetic Reconnection Bubbles near Black Holes
summary: Motivated by the observed horizon-scale polarization variability in multi-epoch Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) data, we develop a time-dependent general relativistic polarized ray-tracing framework to study how localized magnetic reconnection near a black hole imprints itself on synchrotron polarization. We model the reconnection phenomenologically as a transient magnetic bubble. While keeping the underlying spacetime, emission prescription, and polarization transport scheme unchanged, the bubble weakens the local ordered field, reorganizes its geometry, induces a conservative local kinematic response, and relaxes through a finite magnetic-memory prescription. We explore how the key bubble parameters control the recovery of the magnetic-field strength, the spatial spreading of the disturbed region, the persistence of the post-reconnection imprint, and the resulting polarization signatures. Perturbations dominated by different magnetic-field components produce distinct polarized morphologies, EVPA evolution, and Stokes-(Q, U) trajectories: azimuthal perturbations favor outward EVPA shifts, radial perturbations favor inward shifts, and vertical perturbations mainly suppress the polarized intensity. For the illustrative M87^*-like cases, the phase evolution of the β_2 polarization coefficient further traces how localized magnetic reconfiguration contributes to the global EVPA twist of the ring. These results show that horizon-scale polarization variability can provide a sensitive diagnostic of localized magnetic restructuring and that the present framework offers a physically transparent way to interpret time-dependent polarimetric signatures in future EHT observations.

title: CMB Bounds on Primordial Black Holes via Radiation Capture: Linear Perturbations
summary: We investigate the gravitational interaction between primordial radiation, consisting of photons and ultra-relativistic neutrinos, and primordial black holes (PBHs), and study its imprint on the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Assuming that PBHs are immersed in the cosmic radiation background, we introduce a covariant energy-momentum transfer four-vector to describe the gravitational capture of radiation by PBHs. We extend the background-level framework of M. Farhang and S. M. S. Movahed [Phys. Rev. D 114, 083533 (2026)] to an inhomogeneous Universe at linear order by consistently modifying the perturbed continuity and Euler equations to account for both energy and momentum transfer. We use the imprint of this interaction on the CMB to place novel constraints on the PBH abundance, $f_{\rm pbh}$. We show that these constraints are up to two orders of magnitude tighter than those obtained from background-only analyses and exhibit a strong dependence on the PBH mass. Using Planck temperature and polarization data, we constrain the PBH fraction to $f_{\rm pbh} \lesssim 0.05-0.002$ for $M$ in the range $10^{15}-10^{17} M_\odot$. Furthermore, sensitivity forecasts for a cosmic-variance-limited survey with $\ell_{\rm max}=7000$, assuming a fiducial $f_{\rm pbh}=0$, yield projected bounds of $f_{\rm pbh} \lesssim 10^{-2}-2\times 10^{-4}$ over the mass range $10^{13}-10^{17} M_\odot$.

title: SMMAN studies of AGN variability. II. Radio and optical quasi-periodic oscillations and changing variability states in the relativistic jet of the blazar PKS 0754+100
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We report the detection of $\sim$280-day quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the SMMAN observations of PKS 0754+100 at 4.8 and 23.6 GHz, which may also be present in VLBI observations made at 15 GHz. The onset of a transition of the amplitude of variability in the radio flux density, observed more clearly in the 15 GHz and 23.6 GHz observations, coincides with the detection of a likely QPO of $\sim$1.4 days in optical observations made by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. This transition in radio variability also occurs close in time to the disappearance of the secondary knot in the VLBI radio map during the lower variability state. An X-ray flare was observed 100 days before this transition, suggesting that the mechanisms causing these quasi-periodicities are related. After the transition to a higher variability state, both the 15 and 23.6 GHz light curves exhibit indications of QPOs at $\sim$400 days. For the first time, a QPO detected in the radio band from a BL Lac has been seen to appear to shift to a QPO of lower frequency, with that transition occurring near the appearance of a QPO in optical emission at a much shorter period. This multi-waveband behavior could be related to the internal helical structure of the jet, where an instability or kink develops due to magnetic reconnection and propagates outward.

title: Investigating the Viability of Dedicated Microhertz Gravitational Wave Pulsar Timing
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: The microhertz gravitational wave (GW) frequency regime remains one of the least explored regions of the GW spectrum. This is due to the physical limitations of our current and upcoming GW observatories such as LIGO and LISA, which are tuned to dHz and mHz respectively. Proposed experiments targeting the $μ$Hz regime are ambitious, expensive and unlikely to be operational within the next 20 years. Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs), with their Galaxy-sized baselines, occupy the other end of the spectrum; the frequencies they are sensitive to are a function of the observing cadence and total dataset timespan. Existing PTA campaigns have cadences and timespans corresponding to the nanohertz regime, however the possibility exists that they can be 'pushed' to detect higher frequencies. This paper investigates the viability of a custom microhertz-sensitive PTA, observing a small number of millisecond pulsars with a daily cadence, over the course of 1 and 2 years respectively. We assume the use of both 100-m and 500-m class radio telescopes for these observations, and an idealised noise model with negligible systematics to determine the most optimistic detection threshold. We compute the sensitivity of our proposed high-cadence PTA configurations to power-law signals and individual GW sources. We find that a 500-m class telescope would likely be able to set new upper limits on individual sources and GW background signals in the $0.1-1~μ$Hz range; while a 100-m class telescope would, in the best case, only match that of the performance of the EPTA second data release in the same range. Finally we consider a possible $μ$Hz PTA consisting of SKA-Mid and DSA observing 24 pulsars; we find this performs on par with the 500-m class while using far less telescope time, presenting a more feasible solution to microhertz-GW pulsar timing.

title: Self-bound quantum dark fermion stars: saturation, a coupling-capped maximum mass, and tidal signatures of a vector dark sector
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables; submitted for publication
summary: I show that a dark sector whose fermions couple to both a scalar and a vector mediator saturates in close analogy with nuclear matter: the energy per particle develops a minimum at finite density, cold dark matter of this kind is self-bound, and its stars, computed here in full general relativity, possess the sharp surfaces of strange quark stars. Saturation makes the maximum stellar mass a property of the Lagrangian rather than an inheritance of the Chandrasekhar scaling: it rises eightfold across the saturation window, which a critical vector coupling closes, so the theory caps its own maximum mass, at $3.9\,M_\odot$ for a fermion of $1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and the fiducial saturation density, a ceiling shared by the whole family of couplings rather than by any single parameter set. Metastable couplings support two disconnected stable families, one dilute and gravitationally bound, the other dense and self-bound. The quantum-pressure correction, confined by saturation to a surface layer a few Compton wavelengths thick, governs the smallest dark nuggets whilst shifting stellar masses by less than one part in $10^{21}$. A $1.4\,M_\odot$ member of the fiducial family has a radius of $13.3\,\mathrm{km}$, a compactness of $0.155$, and a tidal deformability of $1.6\times 10^{3}$, almost an order of magnitude above the measured neutron-star value, so at a given particle mass and couplings a single well-measured inspiral distinguishes these stars from neutron stars and from their scalar-only counterparts, whilst the deformability surviving at the maximum mass separates them, in principle, from black holes.

title: Ultralight scalar field domain walls and Galileo GNSS atomic clocks
summary: In this article, we study the impact of an Earth-sized ultralight scalar field domain wall (DW) on the European Galileo Global Navigation Satellite System constellation and the feasibility of a related detection. In particular, a set of statistical procedures is developed and implemented to characterize the statistical properties of the background noise for a subnetwork of $N$ Galileo satellite clocks, including a false-alarm rate estimation and a detection efficiency analysis. These methods allow to implement a coincidence analysis and establish a preliminary statistical framework for a robust and controlled search for domain-wall crossings in clock data, and for deriving constraints on the associated fundamental particle physics parameters. The activity is addressed from the point of view of the scientific objectives of the Galileo for Science (G4S$\_2.0$) project.

title: Probing the origin of the LHAASO Peanut with a hidden central accelerator
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: A highly asymmetric, giant Peanut-shaped structure has been detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) in ultra-high-energy gamma rays at high Galactic latitude, $b\approx-17.5^{\circ}$, suggesting anisotropic particle transport around a Galactic accelerator. We investigate whether its spectrum and morphology can arise from a hidden central accelerator embedded in a projected anisotropic halo. The baseline model accounts for the diffuse strip and central excess, while a phenomenological prescription for a localized magnetic field reorientation toward the line of sight (LOS), together with a particle-conserved remapping of the electrons downstream of the far excess into an emitting column of prescribed transverse extent, enhances the emission at the far excess position. We explore various source ages, along with different combinations of ambient magnetic field strength and parallel diffusion coefficient, while accounting for radiative cooling when estimating the viewing geometry. The exploration reveals that relatively rapid parallel transport enhances the far component while preserving a dominant diffuse strip. Representative configurations remain compatible with the observed spectral energy distribution, although the fitted far component remains comparatively weaker than the central component above 100 TeV, even in cases where their component fluxes are comparable at 25-100 TeV. These results illustrate the plausibility of a hidden central accelerator as the origin of the LHAASO Peanut, while identifying the remaining difficulty in reproducing the relative brightness of its compact components within the adopted phenomenological framework.

title: BAO and Type Ia Supernovae in LTB Cosmology: Constraints on Radial Inhomogeneity and Acoustic-Ruler Evolution
summary: We investigate how baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and Type Ia supernovae constrain radial density profiles and acoustic-ruler evolution in Lemaitre-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) cosmology with a cosmological constant. Extending a homogeneous Friedmann-Robertson-Walker analysis requires calculating both distances and unequal radial and transverse stretching of a single initial ruler. Combining transverse BAO with supernovae isolates relative ruler evolution without an absolute calibration, while radial BAO supplies complementary information. We connect this test to exact nonlinear models with a low-density region compensated by surrounding excess matter, varying its depth, width, distance from the observer, and background matter density. Using DESI DR2 BAO and DES-Dovekie supernovae with full covariance and identical calibration freedom, the LTB fit improves $χ^2$ by 8.523 over flat $Λ$CDM for three additional parameters, mainly through the supernovae. DESI strongly rejects the particular deep profile favored by supernovae and angular BAO alone. However, a narrow depression near the observer and a broader, shallower depression farther away fit almost equally well, with $Δχ^2=0.647$. The combined data therefore constrain particular geometries without uniquely reconstructing the density profile or ruler evolution. The inference is conditional on supernova selection and interpreting released BAO summaries through local ruler transport at effective redshifts. Homogeneous simulations show that the fit improvement does not establish a detection of inhomogeneity. Finally, in the local approximation, common LTB ruler evolution shifts angular BAO and the transverse component of three-dimensional BAO together and cannot alone explain their discrepancy.

title: Stochastic Acceleration Downstream of Astrophysical Shocks
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Generation and evolution of turbulence at shock fronts are crucial aspects of the process of particle acceleration in different classes of sources. Here we aim at describing the fate of non-thermal particles and turbulence in the downstream region of an astrophysical shock, both in the case in which turbulence is solely produced upstream and advected through the shock and in the case in which additional turbulence is injected downstream. In particular we will provide an estimate of the effect of stochastic acceleration on particles accelerated at the shock and then advected behind it. The calculations will be specialized to supernova remnant shocks. The temporal evolution of the particle distribution function downstream of the shock and the power spectrum of the turbulent perturbations are both followed by solving numerically the transport equations for the two quantities, accounting for the damping of waves due to the particles that resonantly interact with them, which makes the problem non-linear. Our calculations show that, if waves are only self-generated upstream via Bell instability, they are not able to significantly modify the particle spectrum in the downstream region. Additionally, turbulent cascading in $k$-space quickly drains their energy, further limiting the stochastic acceleration of particles. If, on the other hand, there are additional sources of turbulence downstream, then these waves can contribute meaningfully to second order Fermi acceleration and alter the spectrum of particles. This may reflect in the spectrum of gamma radiation produced through $pp$ scattering downstream. Although second order Fermi acceleration is typically slower than diffusive shock acceleration, particles are expected to stay downstream of shocks for much longer times during which stochastic acceleration can modify their spectrum and affect the spectra of multi-messenger emissions.

title: Gravitational waves and the exit from de Sitter in Inflation without an Inflaton
summary:
In Inflation without an Inflaton (IWI), second-order de Sitter (dS) gravitons generate primordial curvature as the Coulomb-type potential of their gradient stress. Each pair contributes $(p/k)^2$, yielding exponential enhancement over the contributing e-folds. With exact Bunch-Davies evolution, this solution satisfies all four scalar second-order Einstein equations in pure dS. The retarded transverse-traceless solution instead has a UV kernel of order unity, $(k/p)^2$ below the scalar kernel, and a one-loop correction $Δ^2_{h,2}/Δ^2_h\simeq0.04\,Δ^2_h$. Its source acts before internal freeze-out, but oscillatory cancellations prevent tensor enhancement.
  We evolve the curvature through a smooth exit into radiation domination. Conserved curvature resides on the vacuum-decay hypersurface. A global depletion clock holds each scale on zero-shear time for $N_{\rm w}$ e-folds after horizon exit before local release, giving all scales equal enhancement. Energy-momentum conservation feeds the depleted vacuum energy into a non-vacuum sector, modeled as radiation. Deep in radiation domination, $Δ^2_ζ=c_wΔ_h^4e^{N_{\rm w}}/20$, with clock-dependent $c_w$, $n_s-1=-4ε$, and $n_T=-2ε$. The spectrum is adiabatic and Gaussian; super-horizon $ζ$ is conserved to better than $10^{-4}$, and changing the adiabatic exit fluid alters it by less than $0.2\%$. A direct radiation exit requires $31\lesssim N_{\rm w}\lesssim50$, or $3\times10^{-6}\lesssim r\lesssim0.036$.
  At interferometer frequencies, $Ω_{\rm GW}h^2\simeq2\times10^{-21}$--$3\times10^{-17}$, accessible to BBO for $r\gtrsim0.01$ and ultimate DECIGO for $r\gtrsim10^{-5}$; CMB B-mode searches probe $r\gtrsim10^{-3}$. Above $k_{\rm end}e^{-N_{\rm w}}$, the scalar spectrum steepens to $k^{-1}$, suppressing $μ$-distortions for sharp release when $N_{\rm w}\gtrsim45$.

title: The Fate of Collisional Neutrino Flavor Conversion: Fixed Points, Period Doubling, and Chaos
summary: Core-collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers are among the most energetic astrophysical events and promising sources of multimessenger signals. Their dynamics and nucleosynthesis depend sensitively on neutrino transport, yet the impact of neutrino flavor evolution in these dense environments remains poorly understood. Predicting the outcome of collisional flavor instability (CFI) remains a challenge, despite progress in local-relaxation methods for fast flavor conversion. Here we construct homogeneous collective-precession states with stationary flavor populations in two-flavor quantum kinetics with collisional relaxation. The method applies to arbitrary energy spectra and energy-dependent collision rates. Our numerical examples exhibit persistent oscillations and a period-doubling route to chaos. Even in these regimes, the stationary populations estimate the time-averaged flavor populations to within $10\%$ in our tests. These fixed points provide a physically motivated input for incorporating CFI into astrophysical simulations, with implications for neutrino heating and ejecta nucleosynthesis.

title: Coupled dark energy and apparent phantom crossing: a potential-independent lower bound
summary: Baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), combined with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and type Ia supernovae, prefer a dark energy whose equation of state was below $-1$ in the past and is above $-1$ today. A canonical scalar field cannot cross this line, but it can appear to do so if it is coupled to dark matter, and we ask how strong this coupling must be, for any potential. We show that the apparent crossing requires the dark matter to lose a minimum fraction of its mass after recombination, fixed by the expansion history $H(z)$. For a constant coupling $β=d\ln m/dφ$, the mass can change only as fast as the field moves, and the speed of the field is itself set by $H(z)$, so that the coupling must be larger than a minimum value $β_{\rm min}[H(z)]$. This bound holds for any potential, applies to the largest value of the coupling when the coupling depends on the field, and is reached exactly when the field comes to rest within the observed range. For the DESI DR2 best fits, the dark matter must lose about 5-7% of its mass by $z\simeq 0.8$, which requires $β_{\rm min}=0.047$-$0.058$; including the uncertainties of the data, the public DESI DR2 chains give the 95% lower limit $|β|>0.025$-$0.038$. We also apply the bound to published fits of coupled quintessence: all of them respect it, and those with a constant coupling reproduce only a shallow version of the crossing. Since the coupling cannot be smaller than $β_{\rm min}$, two known effects of the coupling have a minimum size: an extra attraction between dark matter particles of at least a few tenths of a per cent of gravity, and a lensing signal at least a few per cent weaker than the clustering of dark matter would suggest.

title: Unveiling a Concentration of Hard X-Ray Point Sources in the Nuclear Stellar Disk with XMM-Newton
summary: The Galactic Center is home to the largest known concentration of X-ray sources ever detected in our Galaxy, including a sizable population of accreting compact objects. Utilizing data from the XMM-Newton Galactic Plane Heritage Survey of the central $20^{\circ}\times2^{\circ}$ of the Milky Way, we investigate the varying source populations in the inner regions of the Galaxy. We identify for the first time a concentration of extremely hard X-ray sources within $|l|<1.3^{\circ}$ and $|b|<0.3^{\circ}$, a region that overlaps the nuclear stellar disk (NSD). We determine that this hardness is intrinsic to the sources and not a manifestation of high line-of-sight column density ($N_{\rm H}$). Unlike the "soft" X-ray sources, this population does not trace the stellar mass distribution, indicating an overabundance compared to the underlying stellar population. We simulate spectra for a variety of source types to model their X-ray hardness and compare their distributions to those we observed in our survey data. We find that a significant subset of the Galactic Center X-ray population may comprise intermediate polars (IPs) with massive white dwarfs, possibly formed through dynamical processes. Our study provides novel observational insights into the distribution of stellar remnants and other X-ray sources in the vicinity of our supermassive black hole, Sgr A*.

title: Little Red Dots from Primordial Black Holes: Non-Gaussianity and Accretion Evade $μ$-Distortion Constraints
summary: Recent JWST observations of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $z \gtrsim 4$ suggest the existence of early supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with masses $\gtrsim 10^6\,M_\odot$. Their rapid emergence challenges conventional seeding and growth scenarios based on accretion and mergers of Population III stellar remnants, motivating renewed interest in primordial black holes (PBHs) formed from primordial perturbations. Explaining such massive seeds requires power spectrum enhancements that are constrained by cosmic microwave background (CMB) spectral distortions. In this work we perform the first comprehensive Bayesian exploration of non-Gaussian primordial perturbations capable of producing SMBH seeds while remaining consistent with CMB spectral distortion constraints, and examine the role of accretion history in constraining these models. We perform a suite of Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses of power spectrum enhancements (lognormal and cut-power-law) with varying local non-Gaussianity and accretion histories, satisfying the COBE/FIRAS $μ$-distortion constraint with and without the requirement that the model produces SMBH seeds. We find that both models can seed LRDs and evade $μ$-distortion bounds for $|f_{\rm NL}|= O(1)$ and peak amplitude $A= O(10^{-3})$, when standard Eddington-limited accretion is also incorporated. Interestingly, the results exhibit a preference for both positive and negative values of $f_{\rm NL}$. The preference for negative $f_{\rm NL}$ is strongly dependent on the accretion history, and is removed if the black holes have a small duty cycle, $f_{\rm duty}\lesssim 0.1$. These results demonstrate that the JWST high-$z$ LRD population can be seeded by primordial perturbations while remaining compatible with CMB data, and highlight the importance of next-generation CMB spectral distortion missions to test this hypothesis.

title: The shape and velocity of black hole coronas
summary: The first highly significant detection of the polarization of the X-rays from the Black Hole X-ray Binary Cygnus X-1 revealed surprisingly strong polarization parallel to its radio jet. The observation is now commonly interpreted as resulting from the Comptonization of some lower frequency seed photons in a laterally extended corona. The emitting plasma is likely moving along the jet axis with a sizable fraction beta of the speed of light, amplifying the polarization degree. In this letter we address the question of how laterally extended the corona actually needs to be to account for the observations, and we calculate the required outflow velocities of velocity-stratified coronas as a function of the stationary-frame aspect ratio h=H/2R of cylindrical coronas of height H and radius R. We find that models with h lesser equal 0.8 and beta=0.5-0.9 at the top of the corona can give both the observed photon index of Gamma=1.6 and the observed 4% polarization parallel to the symmetry axis. We do not find suitable solutions for larger h. Given the constraints on h, we discuss the likely size of the corona, emphasizing that compact coronas close to the black hole are preferred as they can tap more efficiently into the gravitational energy and the rotational energy of the black hole, and are less exposed to their own emission reprocessed in the optically thick portion of the accretion flow.

title: AGN Feedback Turbulence in Cool-core Clusters: Evidence from XRISM
summary: The XRISM X-ray Observatory has revealed evidence for a "double-cascade" scenario in the Perseus cluster, in which active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback and mergers drive turbulence over distinct radial ranges and spatial scales. Whether this gas kinematic feature is common among cool-core clusters remains unclear. Here, we revisit XRISM observations of A1795 and A2029 to investigate the signatures of AGN feedback and their contribution to the gas velocity fields. In A1795, AGN feedback dominates the velocity dispersion in the core, similar to Perseus, and may provide turbulent heating at a rate comparable to radiative cooling. In contrast, we obtain only an upper limit on the AGN feedback contribution in A2029, where merger-driven motions dominate. Tailored simulations indicate that an off-axis minor merger $\simeq1.6$ Gyr ago displaced the central low-entropy gas in A2029, potentially suppressing AGN activity. This gas is now returning to the center, possibly facilitating the re-establishment of AGN feedback. We propose an evolutionary view of the double-cascade scenario, in which merger-driven motions dominate during and shortly after significant mergers, while feedback-driven turbulence re-emerges in cluster cores as systems relax. This framework provides a basis for interpreting XRISM kinematic measurements of (weak) cool-core clusters. Our findings highlight the importance of spatially resolved gas kinematics and detailed modeling for identifying double-cascade features and disentangling the contributions of AGN feedback and mergers.

title: Measurement of the Neutrino Spectrum along the Galactic Plane with IceCube
summary: We present the first measurement of the variation of the high-energy neutrino flux along the Galactic plane using 10 years of neutrino-induced particle-shower data from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. In this Letter, we fit both the neutrino flux normalization and the spectral index, in multiple regions along the plane, independent of model expectations. The neutrino flux per solid angle in the inner Galactic region ($\vert l\vert< 30^{\circ}, \vert b\vert < 8^{\circ}$) is approximately five times higher than in the outer Galactic plane ($\vert l\vert>60^{\circ}, \vert b\vert < 8^{\circ}$) at $E_ν=5\mathrm{TeV}$. The spectral indices in the inner and outer region are $γ=2.76^{+0.18}_{-0.15}$ and $γ= 3.13^{+0.57}_{-0.37}$, respectively. Additionally, we compare the same region of Galactic emission measured in $\mathrm{TeV}$ gamma rays by LHAASO ($15^{\circ}<l<125^{\circ}$) to neutrinos, and conclude that the measurements are compatible within uncertainties, under the assumption of hadronic gamma-ray production.

title: Depth of Maximum of EAS and Mean Mass Composition of Primary CRs from the Spatial and Temporal Distribution of Cherenkov Light According to TAIGA-HiSCORE Data
summary: We present the dependence of the depth of maximum of extensive air showers (EAS), $X_{\max}$, on the energy of the primary particle, as determined from data recorded with the wide-angle Cherenkov array TAIGA-HiSCORE during the 2021--2025 observation seasons. The reconstruction of $X_{\max}$ from the experimental data uses relations obtained from EAS simulations: the dependence on the steepness of the Cherenkov light lateral distribution function ($P$-method) and on the full width at half maximum of the Cherenkov light pulse ($τ$-method). The reconstructed $X_{\max}$ values are converted into the mean logarithmic mass $\langle\ln A\rangle$, which characterizes the primary cosmic-ray mass composition. The results are compared with measurements from Tunka-133 (2017), the Pierre Auger Observatory (2019), LHAASO (2024), TALE (2026), and other experiments.

title: Long before plunge: Uncovering intermediate-mass black holes through their inspiralling compact object companions with LISA
summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will provide novel capability to discover and study intermediate-mass (~$10^2-10^5 M_\odot$) black holes at the centres of dwarf galaxies and in dense stellar environments. We systematically map out the LISA-detectable parameter space of binaries consisting of a low-mass compact object spiralling into an intermediate-mass black hole (mass ratio ~$10^{-5} - 10^{-2}$) on equatorial orbits with generic eccentricity. The depth of the LISA survey reaches a redshift ~$5$ ($0.1$) for binaries with a primary black hole mass $m_1$ ~$10^4 M_\odot$ ($10^3 M_\odot$). If the orbital companion is a white dwarf, which could be disrupted prior to plunge, LISA's survey depth is well matched to (and, in many cases, exceeds) the one of electro-magnetic surveys. Although the maximum distance at which a source can be detected depends weakly on the orbital eccentricity, the latter strongly affects the portion of the binary inspiral over which a source is detectable. The instrument's sensitivity time-volume varies by many orders of magnitude depending on the binary's component masses: it reaches ~$1 - 10^3 Gpc^3 yr$ (~$10^{-2} - 10^3 Gpc^3 yr$) for the more massive systems with $m_1 = 10^5 M_\odot$ ($10^4 M_\odot$) and decreases to ~$10^{-4} - 1 Gpc^3 yr$ for lighter primary black holes with $m_1 = 10^3 M_\odot$. Importantly, from tens of percent to the overwhelming majority of the total sensitivity time-volume (and therefore number of potential detections) comes from sources that do not plunge during the yr-long mission lifetime and are observed at an earlier stage of their inspiral. Despite the poorly known merger rates of this class of sources, our results show that LISA could identify from a handful to ~$10^3$ intermediate-mass black holes providing a new observational avenue for studying these elusive objects and the environments in which they reside.

title: Binary pulsar studies with multi-wavelength sky surveys. II. Companion star follow ups
summary: The identification of the stellar companions to binary pulsars and the extraction of the physical information encoded in their optical spectra are key to study the evolution of the binary system and how this is influenced by the interactions between the two stars. Obviously, extending the characterisation of the companion star spectra over an as large as possible wavelength range allows one to maximise the amount of information. In Paper I, we used 11 source catalogues built upon multi-wavelength (optical, infrared, ultraviolet) imaging sky surveys to search for the stellar companions of 144 field binary pulsars (i.e. not in Globular Clusters) selected from the Australia Telescope National Facility (ATNF) pulsar catalogue. For nine of these pulsars, for which the companion star had been already identified, we obtained new spectral information from imaging photometry in the surveys' bands. In particular, for some of these pulsars we provided the first possible detections of the companion star in either the ultraviolet or mid-infrared. Here, we serve this additional flux information as a base to update the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the companion stars and the multi-epoch catalogue photometry to look for flux modulation at the orbital period of the binary system.

title: A Many-Shapes framework for Galactic Cosmic Rays
summary: Thanks to recent measurements by space and ground-level detectors, the energy spectra of cosmic ray protons and helium nuclei are now known with good precision over a broad energy range extending for more than six orders of magnitude, from a few GeV to approximately 10PeV. These measurements reveal that both spectra do not have a simple power--law form, and exhibit several features. The proton to helium ratio exhibits a very unexpected behavior: it decreases for rigidities $\lesssim 10^5$~GV, and increases for higher rigidities. Several authors have interpreted the observed spectral features as revealing the fact the CR spectra are formed by the contributions of a few components (in some cases as few as two) produced by sources that belong to distinct classes of astrophysical accelerators, with sources in the same class producing spectra with the same characteristic shape. Most of these authors also consider it necessary to include the contribution of one (or perhaps more than one) ``local'' sources, recently active in the vicinity of the solar system. However, this approach has several limitations, and in this work we discuss an alternative scenario in which the cosmic ray sources, even belonging to the same class, produce spectra with a broad range of shapes. The power--law form of the total source spectrum emerges as the average of these contributions. In this framework observable spectral features can be produced by statistical fluctuations, and different spectral slopes for protons and helium nuclei can be observed even if one assumes that acceleration is rigidity-dependent.

title: The Edge of the Warm Corona in Active Galactic Nuclei
summary: A model of warm, dissipative corona on top of an accretion disk is investigated, to explain the soft X-ray excess (SXE) emission observed in active galactic nuclei (AGN). The final ray-traced spectrum, computed through photoionization code with Comptonization, accounts for both: emitted and reflected components. As a result, the strength of the SXE depends on the radial extend of the warm corona, i.e., its outer edge. We show that the radial transition from warm corona to disk atmosphere is governed by line cooling. By moving away from a central black hole Compton cooling is gradually replaced by line cooling, and the temperature drops sharply in vertical direction at a narrow iron ionization front, where iron ions Fe \textsc{xxv}--Fe \textsc{xxvi} recombine to Fe \textsc{xvii}. Notably, this transition takes place at a particular value of internal heating $\approx 1.6 \times 10^{-23}$ erg cm$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, regardless of the Eddington ratio. We show, that at the given metal abundance, the SXE emitting area is larger for a higher accretion rate, in agreement with recent findings in changing look AGN. The overall emission spectrum from a warm corona is featureless, and the only iron K$_α$ line comes from a reflection. The line is stronger and more gravitationally distorted for a lower accretion rate, which is a direct result of the size of the warm corona. Furthermore, by increasing the iron abundance, the iron ionization front moves closer towards black hole, and a stronger iron line complex is emitted locally.

title: GRB 241030A: A fallback-accreting magnetar description of the early X-ray emission
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Accepted in MNRAS
summary: The bright, variable early X-ray emission of GRB~241030A at $z=1.411$ motivates investigating continued central-engine activity before the smoother afterglow emerges. We model a possible underlying magnetar contribution to the unabsorbed 0.3--10~keV XRT flux over 80--430~s, evolving the spin under fallback-disk and electromagnetic torques. A descriptive estimate gives $P_0\simeq4.25$~ms, $B\simeq3.04\times10^{15}$~G and source-frame $t_{\rm fb}\simeq143$~s, with exploratory temporal-block uncertainty ranges. The effective efficiency reaches its geometry-dependent ceiling of 81.2. At observer time 200~s, this realization has $P_*\simeq4.82$~ms and magnetospheric, corotation and light-cylinder radii $r_{\rm m}\simeq235$~km, $r_{\rm co}\simeq48$~km and $r_{\rm LC}\simeq230$~km. It is on the ejector branch; light-cylinder entry near 255~s initiates negative propeller torque and steepens the decline. The smooth component declines throughout the fitted interval; additional variable emission contributes to the observed maximum near 180~s. A correlated-residual Bayesian analysis permits a fainter component and broader dynamical histories, with median $P_0=16.8$~ms and central 68 per cent interval 2.76--286~ms. However, posterior predictive checks reveal that this statistical description typically underpredicts the observed flux level and variability, limiting its physical interpretation. Fallback-modified magnetar activity remains a possible descriptive scenario, but these analyses do not establish a unique underlying component or robust constraints on the initial spin and disk-interaction history. We also discuss Lense-Thirring precession and alternative mechanisms as possible origins of the early X-ray variability.

title: NS 1987A: A Potential Probe of Crustal Superfluidity with Future X-ray Observations
comment: 9+1 pages, 5+1 figures, 2 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Several indirect observations imply that the central compact object in the supernova SN 1987A is likely to be the youngest neutron star identified to date, NS 1987A. We investigate how a future detection of its thermal X-ray emission could constrain neutron-star interiors, using cooling models and a generic high-resolution, large-area X-ray observatory with \textit{Lynx}-like capabilities as a sensitivity benchmark. For the adopted sensitivity and observing window, NS 1987A is detectable at $t\sim60~{\rm yr}$ (roughly 2047) unless rapid neutrino cooling operates, such as the direct Urca process. If the neutron superfluidity in the inner crust is weak, the temperature profile inside NS 1987A is likely not to be isothermal at the detection. In that case, the future direct observation of NS 1987A is a potential probe of the properties inside the inner crust. We compare alternative X-ray observatories and emphasize that both effective area and angular resolution, needed to reduce contamination from the surrounding remnant, determine whether this diagnostic can be realized.
